title: Pangean megamonsoon peaks

facts.text: The Pangean megamonsoon reached its greatest strength in the Triassic, when Pangaea's land area peaked after Siberia and the China cratons joined.
Its circulation may have reversed part of the easterly global winds, sending westerlies onto the west coast.
Shifting winds brought moisture to the previously dry Colorado Plateau.
A greenhouse climate left the continents ice-free, even at the poles.

title: Red Wing impact

facts.text: An impact in what is now McKenzie County, North Dakota, left the Red Wing Creek structure, about 9 km across and now buried some 2,000 m deep.
Thick Jurassic rocks fill the disturbed structure, suggesting a Triassic impact; its age is estimated at 200 ± 25 million years.
It was once grouped with Manicouagan, Saint Martin and Rochechouart as one multiple impact, but those craters proved to be millions of years apart.

facts.text: The Mesozoic marine revolution, a rise in shell-crushing and boring predators and seafloor bulldozing, began with the Mesozoic.
Increasingly capable predators stressed fixed-in-place sea life, shifting the balance as some prey adapted faster than others.
Stalked crinoids were easy prey for shell-crushing predators from the Triassic on.

title: First rhynchosaurs

facts.text: Beaked herbivorous rhynchosaurs appeared in the Induan, shortly after the extinction, within a major diversification of reptiles.
Basal forms such as Noteosuchus come from the earliest Triassic of South Africa's Eastern Cape.
They became most abundant and worldwide in the Carnian, then died out early in the Norian.

title: Anoxic, acidic Early Triassic oceans

facts.text: Oxygen-poor waters persisted through the Early Triassic, which may explain the slow recovery of marine life, especially on the seafloor.
Biomarkers of green sulfur bacteria show hydrogen sulphide reaching sunlit shallow water from the Late Permian into the Early Triassic.
Persistently high carbon dioxide in air and sea hampered the recovery of shell-building organisms.
Alternating oxygen-rich and oxygen-free seafloor conditions may explain carbon-isotope swings of the time.

title: Buntsandstein red beds fill the Germanic Basin

facts.text: Across the Germanic Basin, from England to Poland, arid continental playas laid down the Buntsandstein, red sandstones and conglomerates with little clay.
With the later Muschelkalk and Keuper it forms the three-part Germanic Trias; it holds small reptiles, plants and Chirotherium tracks.
A major late Anisian rise in global sea level flooded the basin with a tropical sea, ending Buntsandstein deposition and starting the Muschelkalk.

title: Coelacanths and lungfishes peak

facts.text: Coelacanths had their greatest burst of diversity in the Early Triassic, just after the Great Dying.
Lungfishes were most diverse during the Triassic; only three genera survive today.

title: Early Triassic hothouse

facts.text: The Early Triassic was the hottest stretch of the whole Phanerozoic, during and just after the Siberian Traps' huge greenhouse-gas release.
Pangaea's interior was mostly hot and arid, with widespread deserts, while the poles stayed temperate.
Equatorial temperatures may have jumped 8–10 °C at the start of the Triassic, to averages of 32–35 °C.
The climate swung repeatedly: a thermal maximum at the boundary, a brief Dienerian cooling (251–249 Ma), then a Latest Smithian Thermal Maximum (about 249–248 Ma).
Extreme heat may have left land between about 30°N and 40°S without tetrapods from the Induan until the early Spathian.

title: First neopterygian fishes

facts.text: The earliest unequivocal neopterygians, including early holosteans, appear near the start of the Triassic, though a Permian origin is suspected.
Ray-finned fishes diversified remarkably, peaking in the Middle Triassic; predators such as saurichthyids grew over 1.2 m long.
Neopterygians diversified later in the Triassic to become leading fish groups in fresh and salt water, and spread through Norian seas as ceratitid ammonites declined.

title: Lystrosaurus dominates land faunas

facts.text: The pig-sized plant-eating dicynodont Lystrosaurus made up as much as 90% of some earliest Triassic land vertebrate faunas.
It was the most common land vertebrate and spread to every corner of Pangaea after the extinction.
Herding, tolerance of extreme, variable climates, very fast growth and early sexual maturity probably explain its success.
Trackways from South Africa's Karoo Basin show dicynodonts were abundant right after the crisis.
Its usual label as a post-extinction disaster taxon has been questioned by some recent evidence.

title: Microbial reefs and mats spread after the extinction

facts.text: Microbial reefs briefly spread across shallow, mostly low-latitude seas in the earliest Triassic, in both oxygen-poor and oxygenated water.
Microbe–animal reefs, built partly by keratinous sponges, dominated many surviving communities and steadied damaged ecosystems.
Microbial mats left wrinkle structures at sea and on land; their later disappearance signals returning burrowers and recovering ecosystems.

title: Siberian Traps pulses recur

facts.text: Carbon-isotope swings and mercury spikes suggest massive Siberian Traps activity recurred several times in the Early Triassic.
These pulses caused further extinctions and may have kept the climate hot; the eruptions persisted into the Early Triassic.
Later Traps activity is linked to the Smithian–Spathian, Olenekian–Anisian and Anisian crises.
A methane release cannot explain the repeated large carbon-isotope shifts.

title: Slow recovery from the end-Permian extinction

facts.text: Life took millions of years to recover from the largest mass extinction, slowed by its severity and the harsh Early Triassic climate.
Successive extinction waves and prolonged environmental stress held recovery back; Early Triassic faunas were poor in species and much alike worldwide.
Seafloor communities stayed low in diversity until the end of the Early Triassic, about 4 million years after the extinction.
On land, ecosystems took about 30 million years to recover; episodes of acidity stunted them well into the Triassic.
Marine recovery then accelerated explosively in the Anisian, as crowded niches sharpened competition.

title: Temnospondyl amphibians rebound

facts.text: Temnospondyls recovered first and peaked in diversity in the early Triassic; most major stereospondyl groups, such as capitosaurs and trematosaurs, appeared then.
Tupilakosaurids thrived as disaster taxa in the Induan; temnospondyls shrank then, but regained pre-extinction sizes in the Olenekian.
Temnospondyls then declined through the Middle and Late Triassic; only brachyopoids and trematosauroids survived beyond it.

title: Moenkopi tidal flats and red beds

facts.text: Rivers, tidal flats and brief marine incursions laid down the Moenkopi's red sandstones and siltstones across the American Southwest, up to about 550 m thick.
Its fossils point to a warm tropical climate, perhaps with monsoonal wet–dry seasons.
Its Early Triassic bivalves, 27 species in 18 genera, cast doubt on the idea that bivalves recovered only in the Middle Triassic.

title: Sea level rises from its Permian–Triassic low

facts.text: Sea level hit its lowest at the Permian–Triassic boundary and stayed low through the Triassic compared with other periods.
Starting near today's level, it rose to about 10–20 m above present during the Early and Middle Triassic.
The rise sped up in the Ladinian, peaking at up to 50 m above today's level in the Carnian.
The Guiyang biota, an exceptionally preserved late Induan assemblage from China's Daye Formation, dates to about 250.8 Ma.
It holds every trophic level of a marine ecosystem, from primary consumers to apex predators.

title: Cynodonts and dicynodonts rebound

facts.text: Only dicynodonts, therocephalians and cynodonts survived among therapsids; cynodonts and dicynodonts soon became dominant, with stocky kannemeyeriiforms the only dicynodonts to thrive.
Cynognathians dominated Early and Middle Triassic cynodonts; Cynognathus was a top predator of Olenekian and Anisian Gondwana.
Cynodonts diversified again around 240 Ma; plant-eating traversodontids peaked in the Late Triassic, mainly in Gondwana.

title: First dinosauromorphs

facts.text: Fossil footprints of dinosauromorphs, the group of dinosaurs and their closest relatives, are known from the Olenekian.
Argentina's Chañares Formation preserves early dinosaur-like ornithodirans such as Lagosuchus and Lagerpeton.
Avemetatarsalians were a minor part of Triassic ecosystems but eventually produced the first pterosaurs and dinosaurs.

facts.text: A new Dicroidium flora took hold around the Induan–Olenekian boundary and peaked in diversity in the Anisian.
Trees of the fern-leaved seed fern Dicroidium dominated large parts of Gondwana during the Triassic.
Dicroidium ecosystems collapsed in the end-Triassic extinction, leaving a relict in Antarctica.
Triadobatrachus massinoti, the earliest known frog, dates from about 250 Ma.
The first lissamphibians, or modern amphibians, appeared in the Triassic; frog forerunners were present by the Early Triassic.
Stem salamanders and caecilians also arose, but lissamphibians became common only in the Jurassic as temnospondyls waned.
Ichthyosaurs evolved from land reptiles that returned to the sea, much as the ancestors of whales and dolphins later did.
Ichthyosaurs first appeared around 250 Ma, just two million years after the end-Permian extinction, among the first marine reptiles.
The oldest ichthyopterygian remains come from the Olenekian of Spitsbergen; early forms lined northern Pangaea's coasts, from Japan and China to Canada.
Ichthyosaurs in the narrow sense arose near the Early–Middle Triassic boundary, about 245 Ma; by the Middle Triassic some were very large.
Ichthyosaurs lasted until about 94 Ma, in the Late Cretaceous.

facts.text: Pangaea reached its height about 250 Ma, at the start of the Triassic.
Around then South China collided with the Qinling complex and North China, joining Pangaea and forming the Sichuan Basin.
The world ocean, Panthalassa, covered almost 70% of Earth's surface.

title: Sonoma orogeny

facts.text: The Sonoma orogeny hit western North America around the Permian–Triassic transition, after the Late Devonian Antler orogeny.
It is linked to the Sonomia island arc or microcontinent accreting onto the continent's western margin.
Some geologists dispute whether converging plates produced it.

contested_note: Some geologists dispute whether convergent plate tectonics produced the Sonoma orogeny.

conflicts.note: Sonomia terrane page puts the accretion in the Middle Triassic

title: East Asia assembles from colliding blocks

facts.text: Annamia, Sibumasu, Qiangtang and Lhasa collided with South China and each other between about 250 and 230 Ma, raising the Indosinian orogeny.
This southern Asian continent then collided, about 240–220 Ma, with North China, Tarim and other blocks along the Central China orogen.
North and South China's collision closed the Qinling ocean; deep subduction destroyed part of the North China craton's root.
Final closure of the Paleoasian Ocean, c. 240–230 Ma, joined Tarim and North China to Kazakhstan and Siberia, forming the Central Asian orogenic belt.
These East Asian blocks gave Pangaea its greatest land area, as climate changed sharply and the megamonsoon developed; any link is still being studied.

facts.text: A second extinction after the end-Permian one, the Smithian–Spathian boundary event, struck during the Olenekian.
It was one of the grim episodes that returned through the Early Triassic and delayed life's recovery.
The late Smithian crisis was a widespread ocean anoxic event; the Smithian ended with a thermal maximum around 249–248 Ma.
Renewed Siberian Traps volcanism and ocean anoxia have been linked to it.
Idaho's Paris biota is the first diverse fossil assemblage known after the event.

facts.text: The Paris biota of Idaho is an exceptionally diverse marine assemblage from the earliest Spathian, about 249 Ma.
It is the first diverse assemblage after the Smithian–Spathian extinction, about 3 million years after the end-Permian one.
Its animals lived in a shallow, near-equatorial sea on Pangaea's west coast; beds with its ammonoids are dated to 248.853 ± 0.086 Ma.

facts.text: Sauropterygians, flipper-limbed marine reptiles, evolved from land ancestors soon after the end-Permian extinction.
The earliest appeared about 248–247 Ma, in the Spathian, and were already notably diverse.
Hupehsuchians, ichthyopterygians and sauropterygians were among the first marine reptiles, entering the scene in the Olenekian.
They flourished through the Triassic; all but the plesiosaurs died out at the period's end.
During the Latest Olenekian Cooling, from 248 to 247 Ma, temperatures fell by about 6 °C.
The Middle Triassic stayed cooler than the Early Triassic, with temperatures falling through most of the Anisian.
Cooler Anisian oceans let animal-built reefs become common again.
A third post-Permian extinction event struck at the Olenekian–Anisian boundary, ending the Early Triassic.
Siberian Traps activity has been linked to it, and to later Middle–Late Anisian and Anisian–Ladinian crises.
Shortly after the Siberian Traps eruptions ended, around 247 Ma, rift valleys began to form; Fundy and Argana basin rift sediments date to 247 Ma.
Extension began in the northern Central Atlantic in the Anisian and the southern part in the Carnian; by 230 Ma new rift valleys had formed and filled.
From about 227 to 202 Ma, deep half-graben basins between New Jersey and Morocco held large rift lakes, red beds and shales, the Newark Supergroup.
Rifting spread to Newfoundland and Iberia, the eastern Mediterranean, and southwestern Gondwana and Patagonia, opening basins such as the Lusitanian and Cuyo.
Three-armed grabens joined into the future Mid-Atlantic Ridge, but Pangaea had not yet separated; Laurasia parted from Gondwana between 215 and 175 Ma.

It is one of a series of Triassic Chinese marine biotas, alongside the older Guiyang biota.

title: First scleractinian corals

facts.text: The first scleractinian (stony) corals appeared in the late Anisian.
Scleractinians are the basis of all Mesozoic and modern reefs.
They diversified rapidly during the Carnian pluvial episode, linked to symbiotic dinoflagellates (zooxanthellae) settling in their tissues.
They did not become the dominant reef builders until the end of the Triassic.
Reefs built by modern-type scleractinian corals first became relatively common in the Carnian.

title: Archosaurs displace therapsids on land

facts.text: Archosaurs, at first rarer than therapsids, began displacing them in the mid-Triassic and were the dominant land vertebrates by the Middle Triassic.
From the early Triassic they took most medium to large land carnivore niches; over 35 million years they came to include crocodylomorphs, pterosaurs and dinosaurs.
Pseudosuchians were ecologically dominant, from plant-eating aetosaurs to big 'rauisuchian' predators; land faunas were shared with dinosauromorphs.
Large cynodonts such as traversodontids still held some big herbivore and predator niches.

Their shapes radiated from the Late Triassic through the Middle Jurassic, when they became prominent phytoplankton.

title: First stem turtles

facts.text: Stem-group turtles date from the Middle Triassic; Pappochelys had no shell but a short torso, broad ribs and long back vertebrae.
In the Late Triassic, Odontochelys had a complete bony plastron but only a partial carapace.
The traits behind the shell may first have helped with digging.

title: Marine reptiles diversify

facts.text: Placodonts, thalattosaurs, Tanystropheus and other marine reptiles joined ichthyosaurs and sauropterygians in the Middle Triassic.
Pachypleurosaurs and nothosaurs were common, especially around the Tethys; Atopodentatus is the earliest known plant-eating marine reptile.
Some nothosaurs reached 5–7 m long, and some ichthyopterygians attained very large body masses.
Almost every known clade of Triassic marine reptile has been found in South China.

title: Middle Triassic recovery and radiation

facts.text: Complex, diverse ecosystems with specialised animals began to re-form in the Middle Triassic, 4–6 million years after the extinction.
Carbon-isotope swings abruptly stabilised in the middle Triassic, soon followed by the recovery of shelled sea life.
Marine reptiles, ray-finned fishes, ammonoids, bivalves and gastropods all reached higher diversity again; crinoids regained ecological dominance.
By the early Ladinian, Chinese lake coprolites show freshwater food webs with six or more trophic levels; phytoplankton, corals and crustaceans had recovered.
Full recovery took about 30 million years; global marine diversity regained pre-extinction levels only in the Middle Jurassic.

title: Tethys gulf extends west into Europe

facts.text: In the Middle Triassic the Tethys, a vast gulf on Pangaea's eastern side, opened farther west at the expense of the shrinking Paleo-Tethys.
Rising seas flooded central Europe as the shallow Muschelkalk Sea, which reached the North Pyrenean Zone.
Rifting that formed the Meliata Ocean basin began in the Anisian.

facts.text: France's Grès à Voltzia, about 245 Ma, preserves varied arthropods, notably detailed myriapods, and the earliest known aphids.
The oldest definite lepidosaur is the rhynchocephalian Agriodontosaurus from England, about 244–241.5 Ma in the late Anisian.
The next oldest rhynchocephalian, Wirtembergia, is Ladinian; the Early Triassic Sophineta may be a lepidosaur relative.
Lepidosaurs, ancestors of lizards, snakes and the tuatara, diversified during the Carnian pluvial episode.

facts.text: The Monte San Giorgio site on Lake Lugano was a Middle Triassic lagoon behind reefs with an oxygen-free bottom, ideal for fossilisation.
Its Besano Formation, about 242 Ma, a World Heritage Site, preserves fish and marine reptiles such as Neusticosaurus and Tanystropheus.
A cooling phase, the Ladinian–Carnian Cooling, followed from 242 to 233 Ma.
Global temperatures were still relatively cool at the start of the Carnian.
Abrupt warming from the Wrangellia eruptions around 234 Ma ended the cooling trend.
The first true flies (Diptera) are known from the Middle Triassic, around 240 Ma, and spread widely through the Middle and Late Triassic.
Flies are one of four great insect radiations; many new species of lower Diptera arose around 220 Ma.
A Triassic fly wing from Mt. Crosby, Australia, is unusually large at 10 mm.

facts.text: The Cimmerian orogeny began about 240–200 Ma as Cimmerian blocks collided with Kazakhstania and North and South China.
Drifting north, the Cimmerian blocks closed the Paleo-Tethys ahead of them and opened the Neo-Tethys behind.
The Paleo-Tethys, open for about 400 million years, had shrunk to a narrow seaway by the Late Triassic, its closure raising the orogeny.
Its western arm stayed open until about 205 Ma, when Iranian blocks hit Eurasia's Turan platform; the belt ran from Anatolia east to the Indosinian orogen.
The Qiangtang terrane of northern Tibet joined Asia in the Late Triassic.

facts.text: Mesozoic marine reptiles suffered their highest extinction rates at the end of the Ladinian, closing the Middle Triassic.
Marine reptiles, like fishes, lost much diversity between the Middle Triassic and the Jurassic.

title: Hyperodapedontine rhynchosaurs spread worldwide

facts.text: Rhynchosaurs diversified around 240 Ma, but lines common in the Middle Triassic died out in the Carnian pluvial episode, leaving specialised hyperodapedontines.
Hyperodapedontines were widespread and abundant in the late Carnian, giving rhynchosaurs their broadest, global distribution.

facts.text: A vast river delta plain spread across northern Pangaea's Triassic Boreal Ocean, today's Barents Sea, from 237 to 227 Ma.
Rapid sedimentation after the extinction had built a shallow basin; Induan silts span 1,000 km of the Greater Barents Sea Basin.
Deposition slowed in the Olenekian–Anisian, revived in the Ladinian with deltas advancing over 500 km, and the plain had formed by 237 Ma.

title: First coccolithophores

facts.text: The oldest known coccolithophores date from the Late Triassic, around the Norian–Rhaetian boundary.
Calcareous nannofossils have a continuous record from the Late Triassic, about 220 Ma, to the present.
One source puts the first coccoliths, with dinoflagellates, in the plankton during the Carnian pluvial episode.
Coccolithophores radiated in the Early to Middle Jurassic, becoming prominent members of the phytoplankton.

facts.text: The earliest probable lepidopteran fossils are scales in herbivore dung about 236 million years old from Argentina, likely swallowed by accident.
Wing scales of Glossata and Micropterigidae-grade moths occur as rare microfossils at the Triassic–Jurassic boundary in a core near Braunschweig, Germany.
Possible stem relatives of caddisflies and moths are known from the Triassic, and the time-scale table lists the first Lepidoptera in the Late Triassic.

facts.text: Wrangellia flood basalts poured onto land over about 5 million years, building a large igneous province now exposed in a 2,500 km belt.
The eruption around 234 Ma caused abrupt global warming that ended the Ladinian–Carnian cooling.
Carbon and osmium isotopes tie it to the Carnian climate upheaval; seawater osmium shifted at the Ladinian–Carnian boundary.
The Wrangellia terrane was later added to western North America.

conflicts.note: Wrangellia terrane page: basalts extruded over 5 million years about 230 Ma (2002–2005 sources)

facts.text: Around 234–232 Ma, for perhaps 1–2 million years, global climate shifted sharply, with major changes to life on land and in the sea.
Volcanism off North America, the Wrangellia large igneous province, set off abrupt global warming that ended the Ladinian–Carnian cooling.
Pangaea's arid climate turned hotter and more humid; rainfall and runoff surged, turning the dry interior into lush alluvial forests.
Carbonate platforms shrank, and many marine invertebrates, especially ammonoids, bryozoans and crinoids, went extinct.
Early dinosaurs, lepidosaurs and possibly mammaliaforms diversified during the event, and coccoliths and dinoflagellates joined the plankton.

facts.text: The earliest true dinosaurs likely appeared in the Carnian, around the time of the Carnian pluvial episode, and diversified rapidly.
Brazil's Santa Maria Formation, radiometrically dated to 233.23 Ma, and Argentina's Ischigualasto Formation, 231–230 Ma, hold early dinosaurs such as Herrerasaurus and Eoraptor.
Nyasasaurus from Tanzania's Manda Formation hints that dinosaurs may date back to the Anisian, about 243 Ma.
They arose from avemetatarsalians, a minor part of Triassic ecosystems, and became dominant only in the Jurassic.
Whether the Carnian pluvial episode drove their rise is doubtful: avemetatarsalian diversity grew faster in the Ladinian and Norian.

facts.text: Early sauropodomorphs such as Buriolestes and Saturnalia come from Brazil's Santa Maria Formation, dated to 233.23 Ma.
Eoraptor, once grouped with herrerasaurids, is now seen as an early sauropodomorph.
Timeline of Earth lists the earliest sauropods at about 233 Ma; quadrupedal sauropodomorphs appeared later in the Late Triassic.
In a reactivated half-graben rift basin in northwestern Argentina, rivers from volcanic highlands laid down sandstones, mudstones and ash beds up to about 1 km thick.
Rainfall was strongly seasonal; one study traces a shift from warm, humid conditions to drier ones around 229.5 Ma, with partial recovery by 227.8 Ma.
Dense with fossils, it is a konzentrat-lagerstätte with some of the earliest unambiguous dinosaurs, such as Herrerasaurus and Eoraptor, amid abundant rhynchosaurs and cynodonts.

facts.text: The first theropods, the meat-eating dinosaur line, appeared about 231 Ma.
Carnian dinosaurs include early theropods as well as sauropodomorphs.
More advanced theropods, the neotheropods, first appeared later in the Late Triassic.

facts.text: Virginia's Cow Branch Formation, about 230 Ma, preserves a wide range of fish, reptiles, arachnids and insects.
Kyrgyzstan's Madygen Formation, about 230 Ma, has yielded over 20,000 fossil insects, one of the richest Triassic Lagerstätten.
It also holds fish, amphibians, reptiles and synapsids, including the earliest drepanosaurid, Kyrgyzsaurus.
Pterosaurs evolved about 228 Ma, a little after the first true dinosaurs.
Like dinosaurs, they arose from avemetatarsalians, which were a minor part of Triassic ecosystems.
Feathers may already have been present in the Early Triassic common ancestor of pterosaurs and dinosaurs.
Early long-tailed pterosaurs appeared in the Norian and quickly spread worldwide.
Norian lagoon deposits in northern Italy, such as the Calcare di Zorzino (c. 216.6–212 Ma), preserve pterosaurs and other reptiles.

facts.text: An impact in what is now Manitoba, Canada, left the Saint Martin structure, about 40 km across.
It was once grouped with Manicouagan and Rochechouart as one multiple impact, but its 227.8 ± 1.1 Ma age shows the craters formed millions of years apart.

title: End-Carnian extinction

facts.text: Several plant-eating archosauromorph groups died out, and big herbivorous therapsids such as kannemeyeriid dicynodonts dwindled across Laurasia.
Repeated floods drowned the vast Triassic Boreal Ocean delta plain, shifting shorelines over 1,000 km and wiping out many of its organisms.
Coastal habitat loss hit semi-aquatic crurotarsans, the dinosaurs' main rivals, and a reef crisis struck South China.

contested_note: Sources hedge on whether a distinct end-Carnian extinction happened, partly because the Carnian–Norian boundary age is disputed.

conflicts.note: 'Short-Norian' view puts the Carnian–Norian boundary, and so this turnover, near 220 Ma

facts.text: Rhynchocephalians, relatives of the living tuatara, had spread worldwide by the end of the Carnian.
They went on to be the dominant small reptiles of the Jurassic.

title: Chinle Formation laid down

facts.text: Rivers, lakes and floodplains, with much volcanic ash, laid down the colourful Chinle Formation across the American Southwest.
Exposed in Petrified Forest National Park and the Painted Desert, it holds a unique late Carnian–early Norian land record.
U-Pb dating and magnetostratigraphy confirm a Norian age for the lower Chinle.

title: Dinosaurs diversify in the Norian

facts.text: Plant-eating sauropodomorphs diversified in the Norian and began to displace large herbivorous therapsids, perhaps coping better with growing aridity.
Plateosaurus, an early sauropodomorph, evolved around 214 Ma in Europe, Greenland and North America.
Most Triassic dinosaurs were small predators; Coelophysis, 1–2 m long, was one of the few common ones.
Crurotarsan archosaurs still filled more ecological niches than dinosaurs.

title: Last rhynchosaurs

facts.text: Hyperodapedontine rhynchosaurs, abundant beaked plant-eaters, died out in the early Norian.
Teyumbaita from Brazil is the only rhynchosaur known with confidence to have survived into the Norian.
Their exact extinction date is uncertain: they lasted at least into the early to middle Norian, though one suggestion places it in an end-Carnian extinction.

title: Mid-Norian marine extinction

facts.text: A marine extinction in the middle of the Norian struck radiolarians, sponges, conodonts and Triassic ammonoids.
It has been blamed on the Manicouagan impact, which may also have hastened the decline of conodonts and ammonoids toward their end-Triassic extinction.

title: Sea level falls to a Rhaetian low

facts.text: After a Carnian high of up to 50 m above today's, sea level fell from the Norian onward.
It bottomed out about 50 m below present in the mid-Rhaetian, and low levels lasted into the earliest Jurassic.
With no evidence of Triassic ice sheets, glaciation is unlikely to explain these sea-level changes.
At the very end of the Triassic the sea flooded most of central and western Europe, turning it into an archipelago.
A sea-level drop seen in Europe and the Middle East at the extinction now seems regional rather than global.

title: First mammaliaforms

facts.text: Mammaliaforms, mammals plus their closest extinct kin, arose from advanced probainognathian cynodonts in the Late Triassic; some sources place their origin in the Carnian.
Unambiguous mammaliaforms such as morganucodonts and haramiyids appeared in the Norian across Europe and Greenland, as probainognathians became prominent.
The oldest claimed forms are doubtful: Tikitherium may be a misidentified Cenozoic shrew, and Adelobasileus is no older than 225 Ma.
Early mammaliaforms were small, mostly nocturnal, warm-blooded insectivores in the shadow of dinosaurs; old jaw bones were moving into the middle ear.
Cynodonts were the only therapsids to outlast the Triassic, and mammaliaforms diversified widely in the Jurassic.

contested_note: Sources disagree on timing: some studies place mammal origins in the Carnian pluvial episode, others in the Norian or at the end of the Triassic.

facts.text: A relatively cool spell, the Early Norian Cool Interval, lasted from about 227 to 217 Ma.
It followed the Mid-Carnian Warm Interval that the Carnian pluvial episode had ushered in.
At the Carnian–Norian boundary, a positive carbon-isotope excursion suggests more organic carbon was being buried.
Teleosts, the group of most modern ray-finned fishes, first appear around 225 Ma.
Early stem teleosts such as Prohalecites lived in the western Tethys; teleosts now make up over 99% of living ray-finned fishes.

facts.text: Warmer conditions, the Mid-Norian Warm Interval, followed from about 217 to 209 Ma.
Around 214 Ma it was briefly interrupted by a cooling possibly linked to the Manicouagan impact.
Around 212 Ma, a peak in orbital eccentricity made much of Pangaea swampy and shrank its arid zones.
An asteroid about 5 km wide struck what is now Quebec, excavating a multiple-ring crater about 100 km across, among Earth's largest.
It was the second-largest impact of the Mesozoic, after Chicxulub.
Shocked-quartz ejecta from it is found as far away as England and Japan.
It may have caused a brief cooling, a mid-Norian marine extinction and the Adamanian–Revueltian turnover, but direct evidence is lacking.
Some 13 million years older than the Triassic–Jurassic boundary, it is no longer thought to have caused the end-Triassic extinction.

title: Adamanian–Revueltian faunal turnover

facts.text: In the American Southwest, several land vertebrates vanished quickly around 215 Ma as others appeared, a turnover in the Chinle Formation.
Trilophosaurus, Desmatosuchus, dicynodonts and many phytosaurs disappeared locally; new aetosaurs and phytosaurs replaced them.
Pollen shifted to dry-adapted plants, suggesting rising aridity; the Manicouagan impact is one proposed cause.

contested_note: Its cause and importance are debated; it may have been only a small, local extinction.

facts.text: Argoland, on Australia's northern margin, began to break into microcontinental fragments around 215 Ma.
It fragmented during Late Triassic rifting that pulled the Lhasa terrane away from Gondwana.
A major Norian rifting episode, about 210 Ma, split Gondwana in two parts.
The earliest true turtles, such as Proganochelys and Proterochersis, appeared in the Norian.
Proganochelys completed the shell, with a fully developed carapace and plastron.
The split between side-necked and hidden-necked turtles, ancestors of all living turtles, is estimated at about 210 Ma.

facts.text: About 215 Ma, a range of basal archosauromorphs, including the protorosaurs, died out.
It was the first of two Triassic extinctions that removed most of the early dinosaurs' competitors.
Early dinosaur lineages diversified through the Carnian and Norian, possibly filling the emptied niches.
A cooler phase, the Rhaetian Cool Interval, lasted from about 209 to 201 Ma.
The Triassic closed with an extreme warming, the End-Triassic Thermal Event, blamed for the mass extinction.

title: Rochechouart impact

facts.text: An asteroid hit what is now western France near Limoges, leaving the Rochechouart structure, about 23 km across.
It struck an island on the edge of the Massif Central near the sea, probably raising a large tsunami.
Though a few million years before the Triassic–Jurassic boundary, it seems too small to have caused the mass extinction.

contested_note: Its age has long been debated, with estimates from under 150 to over 240 Ma; recent dates converge on 203–207 Ma.

facts.text: Shastasaurian ichthyosaurs reached huge sizes in the Carnian and Norian; Shonisaurus grew to 15 m.
These giants seem to have vanished at the end of the Norian, as ichthyosaur variety declined.
Growing competition from sharks, teleost fishes and the first plesiosaurs may explain the decline.

title: Norian–Rhaetian extinction

facts.text: An extinction near the Norian–Rhaetian boundary hit ammonoids, bivalves, conodonts and radiolarians; almost all species of the once worldwide large bivalve Monotis vanished.
A sharp negative carbon-isotope spike in Tethyan and Panthalassan sections is tied to it; the last Monotis lie between ash beds dated 205.70 and 205.30 Ma.
The Angayucham large igneous province in Alaska or the Rochechouart impact may have caused it, but its dating and effects are uncertain.

contested_note: One source calls it an alleged, much smaller extinction, and the Rhaetian page says its dating and effects on life are uncertain at best.

title: Marine life declines before the end-Triassic crisis

facts.text: Gastropods suffered steady losses through the late Norian and Rhaetian, and offshore bryozoans had declined since the Norian.
Anoxia struck northeastern Panthalassa during the Rhaetian, and the carbon cycle was disturbed before the main crisis.
Mean annual temperatures rose 7–9 °C from the late Norian into the Rhaetian.

facts.text: Igneous activity of the Karoo large igneous province began about 204 Ma on its northern margin.
The Karoo-Ferrar flood basalts are later tied to the Toarcian extinction of the Early Jurassic.
Plesiosaurs first appeared in the latest Triassic, possibly in the Rhaetian, about 203 Ma.
At least six plesiosaur lineages crossed into the Jurassic, while all other sauropterygians died out.
They became especially common in the Jurassic and lasted until the end-Cretaceous extinction.

facts.text: As central Pangaea rifted, vast eruptions began: the first CAMP lavas date to 201.566 ± 0.031 Ma, the last to 201.36 ± 0.02 Ma.
CAMP is Earth's largest continental igneous province, about 11 million km² on four continents, with 2–6 million km³ of lava.
Lava came in four main pulses, each lasting no more than about 100 years, spread over some 600,000 years.
It ended the long rifting of the Central Atlantic; large magma bodies had built up about 100,000 years before the eruptions.
It is widely blamed for the Triassic–Jurassic extinction; the link became firmer in 2013.

facts.text: An extreme warming, the End-Triassic Thermal Event, struck at the very end of the Triassic and drove the mass extinction.
Carbon dioxide bubbles in CAMP basalts show the volcanism helped trigger it.
CAMP pulses released carbon over mere centuries, inviting comparison with today's human-caused warming.
Longer-term warming and ocean acidification followed the eruptions, and a thermal spike marks the start of the Jurassic.
One of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions ended the Triassic 201.4 million years ago; about 46–72% of marine genera disappeared.
On land most archosaurs except crocodylomorphs, pterosaurs and dinosaurs died out, with most therapsids and large amphibians; one estimate puts tetrapod losses at 42%.
Ammonites were nearly wiped out, conodonts vanished and reefs collapsed, completing the oceans' shift to the modern evolutionary fauna.
Floras turned over, with 17–73% of Rhaetian plants lost by various estimates, though some see restructuring rather than a plant mass extinction.
Driven by CAMP volcanism and the warming it caused, it removed the crurotarsans and let dinosaurs dominate the Jurassic.

facts.text: Black shales and a sharp negative uranium-isotope shift show marine oxygen fell steeply during the extinction.
Anoxia reached the western and eastern Tethys and Panthalassa, and persisted into the Hettangian as land nutrients fed the seas.
Malformed nannoplankton and a worldwide pause in carbonate deposition point to severe ocean acidification.
Green sulphur bacteria, which photosynthesise with hydrogen sulphide, grew markedly across the boundary.
It is the best-established case of a marine mass extinction caused by acidification, selectively killing organisms with thick aragonite skeletons.
Dicynodonts, among the most successful Permian therapsids, stayed large plant-eaters until they died out at the end of the Triassic.
Their last appearance is uncertain; they survived at least into the late Norian or earliest Rhaetian.

facts.text: Phytosaurs and aetosaurs, common in Late Triassic faunas, were completely wiped out by the end-Triassic extinction.
Among pseudosuchians only small crocodylomorphs survived; herbivores like aetosaurs and carnivorous rauisuchids died out.
Timing is hard to pin down: the Rhaetian and Hettangian hold few large land animals, and some groups may have vanished earlier.
